title: The Hidden Work of Growth #2: Don't Take It Personally
author: Elina
summary: In the second installment of her Hidden Work of Growth series, executive coach Elina uses a composite client case, Fiona, a helpful, agreeable professional who plateaus once being useful stops being enough for further growth, to argue that the common advice "don't take it personally" is nearly useless because it targets the wrong link in the causal chain. Tracing the sequence from external event to internal reaction, she isolates a hidden middle step, interpretation, showing that the same interruption reads as disrespect, undermining, or dismissal only because of an unverified story the mind builds automatically, and that the emotional reaction, however intense, is actually responding to that interpretation rather than to the bare event itself. Her first reframe asks people to pause at the moment of interpretation and ask what evidence actually supports the story before treating it as fact; her second reframe distinguishes emotional self-regulation from emotional suppression, arguing the capability that matters is decoupling emotion from immediate decision, using anger or hurt as information rather than either acting on it unfiltered or shaming it into silence. The piece closes by redefining professional toughness itself as maturity, a combination of emotional self-regulation, perspective-taking, and relational agency, rather than the absence of feeling, concluding that "you cannot practise not taking things personally. You can practise creating more space between what happens and how you choose to respond."
points: Elina's core diagnostic move locates a hidden step between event and reaction, interpretation, showing that identical actions (being interrupted, being challenged) produce identical emotional intensity only because of an automatic, unverified story ('they don't respect me') the mind attaches to them before the feeling even registers.

Her distinguishing of emotional self-regulation from emotional suppression is precise and clinically useful: 'self-regulation is not just about using all your willpower to show up calm and collected while you are crying or shouting inside. It is also the capability to decouple emotions from decisions,' treating anger and hurt as information rather than as either instructions to act on or shame to suppress.

The redefinition of 'professional toughness' as maturity rather than emotional absence gives the piece a genuinely actionable three-part framework, emotional self-regulation, perspective-taking, and relational agency, that a leader can practice individually rather than treating toughness as a fixed trait one either has or lacks.

The closing line reframes the entire piece's practical target with precision: 'you cannot practise not taking things personally. You can practise creating more space between what happens and how you choose to respond,' converting a vague piece of career advice into a specific, trainable skill.
quotes: And when she puts something on the table and gets interrupted once, twice, she shuts down and withdraws: Why bother trying?

Someone interrupts, they don't respect me. Someone challenges, they are trying to undermine me. Someone doesn't engage, they have already decided they don't want to listen. And it's the interpretation that often shapes and intensifies the emotional response.
What if we stop at step one and, before we build a story, ask: What evidence do I actually have before I decide what this interaction means?

Self-regulation is not just about using all your willpower to show up calm and collected while you are crying or shouting inside. It is also the capability to decouple emotions from decisions. The anger and hurt are information.

It is not a capability of not feeling and being strong and assertive no matter what life throws at you. Behind real professional maturity, there is a different set of capabilities that you can develop and practise: Emotional self-regulation: you know what's happening with you in the moment, without being overwhelmed by it.
You cannot practise not taking things personally. You can practise creating more space between what happens and how you choose to respond.
